card.hook: Picture a flat, calm lake with Machhapuchhre sitting upside down in the water, and a little boat drifting through the middle of it. That's the Phewa Lake shot, and it works even on a basic phone.
card.stand_here: Stand on Lakeside Road at the eastern end of Lakeside, near Hotel Barahi Point. Face west toward the lake, then turn north to catch the Annapurna and Machhapuchhre peaks across and along the water.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the whole shoreline and sky, then switch to 1x for a cleaner, less stretched view of lake and mountains. Try 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) for the island temple or the distant peaks.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and put the horizon on the upper third if the mountains are the star, or the lower third if the reflection is. Add a moored boat or a bit of shoreline in the foreground for depth.
card.best_time: Early morning is your best chance of still water and clearer mountains, because haze and cloud tend to build later in the day. If the peaks hide in cloud, shoot boats, reflections and the shoreline instead.
card.selfie_here: On the lakeside promenade beside Hotel Barahi Point, turn your back to the water, use the front camera at 0.5x and let the lake sit behind your shoulder. It's the easiest spot to reach on foot, but it's usually crowded, so be patient for a gap. For a bigger backdrop, Phewa Lake View Point is a short hike away and frames the lake and hills together.
card.ask_someone: At the World Peace Pagoda (Shanti Stupa) on Ananda Hill, stand on the hilltop with the whole lake behind you and ask a passer-by to take the photo from the pagoda area.
card.rules_and_safety: Boat trips and visits to the island temple of Tal Barahi are separate from the promenade walk and need a boat, usually arranged in advance.
card.challenge: Get a boat, the island temple and a mountain peak into one frame, then tell everyone you planned it.
card.good_to_know: Phewa is the third largest lake in Nepal, sitting at about 742 m above sea level and covering roughly 5.7 square kilometres. The Annapurna range is only about 28 km away in a straight line, and the lake is well known for mirroring Machhapuchhre when the water is still. Out on the water, Tal Barahi is a two-storey temple on an island.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on Lakeside Road at the eastern end of Lakeside, near Hotel Barahi Point. Face west toward the lake, then turn north to catch the Annapurna and Machhapuchhre peaks across and along the water.

card.hook: Picture a hilltop in the dark, a crowd of people holding up their phones, and then the first light touches Annapurna, Dhaulagiri and Machhapuchhre. That's a normal morning at Sarangkot, and it's worth the early alarm.
card.stand_here: Stand about 930 m west of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face east. You'll look out at the sunrise light on the peaks, with Phewa Lake and the Pokhara valley spread out below you.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the whole range, the lake and the valley into one shot. Switch to 1x to get the tower steps or railings in the front of the picture, then try 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out a single peak like Machhapuchhre.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the brightest part of the sky, then slide the brightness down a little (darker) so the snow keeps its detail.
card.best_time: Sunrise, and get there before it starts. One reviewer reached the tower just before 5:30 AM and said the crowd grew quickly after that. Cloud can hide the mountains, especially in the monsoon months.
card.selfie_here: Take it on the steps in front of the Sarangkot View Tower, on the side facing the mountains. Use the front camera at 0.5x and hold your phone a bit low, so the tower and the Annapurna view fit over your shoulder. The main lookout beside the tower is a good backup, with the panorama of Pokhara and Phewa Lake behind you.
card.ask_someone: If you're over at Shanti Stupa in Pokhara, ask a passer-by to snap you there with Sarangkot hill and the big mountains behind you across the lake.
card.rules_and_safety: Bring a flashlight in case you walk back in the dark. The View Tower is reported to charge an entry fee (the amount is reported differently), and some sources say it can be closed for maintenance, so check on arrival.
card.challenge: Get a paraglider and a snow peak in the same frame, then try to look as calm as the pilot.
card.good_to_know: Sarangkot is a hill about 1600 m high on the western side of Pokhara, and it's the standard place to watch the sunrise over the Himalaya. It's also known for Manaslu views and as one of the best paragliding spots in the world. If the tower is crowded or you'd rather skip the fee, the free area beside the Panchmukhi Ganesh Temple is also recommended for sunrise or sunset. You can also hike up from Miruwa on the Pokhara Baglung highway in about 90 minutes.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand about 930 m west of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face east. You'll look out at the sunrise light on the peaks, with Phewa Lake and the Pokhara valley spread out below you.

card.hook: Most waterfalls end in a pool. This one just vanishes into the rock, like the mountain swallowed it. Your photo is all about catching that disappearing act.
card.stand_here: Stand right at the subject, on the viewing platforms and railed cliff path at the top of the falls, at the beginning of the path. Face the gorge so you can see the white water plunge and start to slip into the rock tunnel.
card.zoom: Start at 1x to get the whole drop in one shot. If the platform is packed, try 0.5x to squeeze in the railings and the gorge, or go 2x to pick out the white water against the dark rock.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, put the main stream along one vertical line and let the gorge wall fill the other side.
card.best_time: The monsoon (June to September) gives the strongest flow, so the falls look their most dramatic. October to November or March to May may give clearer views.
card.selfie_here: Head to the small wishing pond right next to the falls, where visitors toss coins. Use the front camera at 0.5x and step back a little so the water has a chance to sneak in over your shoulder, though it won't line up perfectly. For a fun fallback, pose with the row of statues in traditional Nepali dress.
card.ask_someone: The front viewing area just past the ticket counter shows most of the falls, so it's a good spot to hand your phone to a friendly passer-by.
card.rules_and_safety: The steps can be slippery, so wear sturdy shoes and take extra care after rain. The falls may be ticketed and a temporary closure has been reported, so check current opening status before you go.
card.challenge: Catch the exact moment the stream disappears into the rock, with the white water on one gridline and the gorge on the other.
card.good_to_know: In Nepali it's called Patale Chhango, the "Underworld's Waterfall". The water runs through a tunnel about 150 m long, roughly 30 m below ground, then passes through Gupteshwor Mahadev Cave. The English name comes from a Swiss visitor who died here in 1961, when her father asked for the fall to be named after his daughter.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand right at the subject, on the viewing platforms and railed cliff path at the top of the falls, at the beginning of the path. Face the gorge so you can see the white water plunge and start to slip into the rock tunnel.

card.hook: Picture a river that rushes through a mossy rock channel, throws a white fuss, and then just disappears underground. That's the show at Devi's Falls, and it's a lot more dramatic than a cave car park has any right to be.
card.stand_here: Stand at Patale Chhango, the falls across the road from the cave entrance, about 180 m to the north-east of it. Face the falls from the road side, so the white water and the mossy channel fill your screen.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to get the falls and the whole channel in one go. Then try zoom 2x or more (depends on your phone) to pick out the rushing water and the rock texture, so you don't have to lean over any barrier.
card.make_it_pop: Tap on the rock beside the falls, then drag the slider down so the picture gets a little darker and the water doesn't turn into a plain white blur.
card.best_time: No time of day is guaranteed here, so go when the road side isn't crowded. The viewing area may close during the monsoon because of flooding, so check before you head over.
card.selfie_here: Take it on the spiral staircase just outside the main Shiva shrine at the cave entrance, which is outside the area where photos are banned. Use the front camera at 0.5x and keep the curving staircase over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the Davis Falls gate side of the highway and frame you with the cave entrance across the road, and cross that busy road with care.
card.rules_and_safety: Photos aren't allowed at the main Shiva shrine inside the cave, and caretakers enforce it. Flash is prohibited inside, and guides disagree on whether photos are OK elsewhere in the cave, so shoot outside and at the entrance unless staff clearly say otherwise. The metal staircase and rocky ground near the waterfall are slippery, so take it slowly.
card.challenge: Turn on gridlines and run the water along one line, with green rock on both sides, so it leads the eye right into your photo.
card.good_to_know: The cave is in Chhorepatan, Pokhara-17. Devi's Falls, also called Davis Falls, passes through the cave, so the falls and the cave make a natural pair. Great Himalayan leaf-nosed bats and fruit bats have been recorded inside, and a British scientific expedition catalogued the animals there in 1976.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand at Patale Chhango, the falls across the road from the cave entrance, about 180 m to the north-east of it. Face the falls from the road side, so the white water and the mossy channel fill your screen.

card.hook: Most temples make you walk up to them. This one sits out on its own island in Pokhara's lake, so your best shot is a view across the water, with boats bobbing in front.
card.stand_here: Stand on the Lakeside promenade near Hotel Barahi Point and face east, straight out across the open water. The temple island will be right there in front of you, with the shoreline and boats in the foreground.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the whole scene of shore, boats, water and island. Then try zoom 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) to bring the roofs closer, and tuck your elbows in to keep the shot steady.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the island, then drag the brightness slider down a little (darker) so the sky and water keep their colour.
card.best_time: Early morning is a sensible bet, since the promenade is likely to be quieter and the water may be calmer. Light changes with the weather, so check how it looks on the day.
card.selfie_here: If you take a boat across, try the courtyard outside the shrine, with the temple behind you. Use the front camera, try zoom 0.5x, and keep the temple over your shoulder. No exact selfie spot is marked, so look around when you arrive.
card.ask_someone: On the Lakeside shore (the boat departure area), ask a passer-by to stand facing the water while you stand with the island and temple in view across the lake behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Photos are fine outside the temple but restricted inside the sanctum. Take your shoes off before entering the shrine and dress modestly. Be careful boarding and leaving the boat, especially with children.
card.challenge: Turn on the gridlines, put the horizon on a lower line, and catch a boat in the foreground with the island floating behind it.
card.good_to_know: Tal Barahi Temple sits on a small island in the lake off Lakeside, Pokhara. The promenade is the easiest place to see it, but it can get crowded, so wait for a gap. To see it up close with the mountains and their reflections behind it, you need a boat, so ask locally about the crossing. For a quieter view, try Pame, where you can see fishing activity with the island across the water.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on the Lakeside promenade near Hotel Barahi Point and face east, straight out across the open water. The temple island will be right there in front of you, with the shoreline and boats in the foreground.

card.hook: Picture a bright white dome against open sky, with a golden tip on top and a whole lake city laid out behind you. That's Shanti Stupa on Anadu Hill, and it's one of the easiest wide views in Pokhara.
card.stand_here: Stand right at the subject, on the main platform in front of the stupa. Face the white dome for the pagoda shot, then turn round to look over Phewa Lake and the Pokhara Valley.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to get the whole pagoda in. Try zoom 0.5x to fit in the tiers and lots of sky, and zoom 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out the golden tip, the Buddha statues or the far-off mountains.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the pagoda, then slide it a little darker so the white stone keeps its detail, and switch on gridlines to put the dome on one vertical line.
card.best_time: Sunrise and sunset are the best times, because the hilltop is known for both. The Annapurna range shows up on a clear day.
card.selfie_here: Take it on the main platform in front of the stupa, with the lake and valley below you. Use the front camera, try zoom 0.5x, and hold the phone a bit low so the white pagoda sits over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the steps below the stupa, while you stand up on the steps or path above, so they can fit the whole stupa behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Photos are welcome but video is restricted here, so stick to stills and check the current rules at the entrance. One visitor reported warnings of muggings on the trekking route, so take care there. The same visitor found the stairs up to the pagoda safe.
card.challenge: Get the golden tip on top and the dome's clean curve in one shot, with not a single stranger in the frame (patience is part of the game).
card.good_to_know: The foundation stone was laid on 12 September 1973, and the pagoda was inaugurated on 30 October 1999 after years of delays. It's about 115 feet tall, and the four Buddha statues on the second tier were given by Japan, Sri Lanka, Thailand and Nepal. The hill sits about 1100 metres above sea level.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand right at the subject, on the main platform in front of the stupa. Face the white dome for the pagoda shot, then turn round to look over Phewa Lake and the Pokhara Valley.

card.hook: Most caves make you work for the photo in the dark. Mahendra Cave does the opposite: the best picture is at the doorway, before you've even gone down a single step.
card.stand_here: Stand right at the cave mouth at the top of the stairs, facing the entrance, so the stone steps drop away into the limestone passage behind your subject.
card.zoom: Use zoom 1x for a person standing in the cave mouth, which keeps the entrance looking natural. Switch to zoom 0.5x for the stairs, where space is tight, and keep your phone level so the walls don't lean.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines to centre your friend in the opening, then tap their face, and if the bright outside makes the entrance glare, drag the slider to make it a little darker.
card.best_time: Go in daylight, when the entrance is bright and your friend is easy to see. A softly overcast moment or shade at the mouth is easier for a phone to handle.
card.selfie_here: Try the wooden steps where the descent begins near the entrance gate, where the painted Shiva-Parvati murals make a colourful backdrop. Use the front camera at zoom 0.5x and let the murals sit over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand at the top of the spiral stairs on the garden side, where the stairway and entrance are both in view, while you pose in the cave mouth.
card.rules_and_safety: Photography may be restricted on the stairs, so look for signs and ask staff. Skip the flashlight and follow the guidelines posted at the entrance. The stairs inside can get wet and slippery from dripping limestone, so watch your step.
card.challenge: Get one shot where the stone steps lead the eye down behind your friend, with the gridlines lined up so nothing leans.
card.good_to_know: Shepherds found Mahendra Cave in the 1950s, and it was once called 'Adhero Bhawan', meaning Dark Habitat. It got its present name after King Mahendra inaugurated it. It's a rare Nepali cave with both stalactites and stalagmites, and there's a statue of Shiva inside.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand right at the cave mouth at the top of the stairs, facing the entrance, so the stone steps drop away into the limestone passage behind your subject.

card.hook: Picture a bronze statue right next to you, a climbing wall replica just behind it, the museum building in the middle and, if you're lucky, a row of Himalayan peaks standing over the roof. That's three layers in one photo, and your phone loves it.
card.stand_here: Start at the phone icon on the map, about 190 m south-west of the subject, and face north-east towards the International Mountain Museum. Then wander up to the entrance grounds by the climbing wall replica and the statues for your close-up shots.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the building, the climbing wall replica and the statues into one frame. Switch to 1x for a tidier shot of a single statue with the building behind it. On a clear day, try 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) to bring the mountains closer.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and put the horizon on the upper line so the mountains get plenty of room.
card.best_time: Pick a clear day, when the mountains are most likely to show above the building. If it's cloudy, let the statues and the climbing wall be the stars instead.
card.selfie_here: Stand beside the large white Manaslu model, on the left of the path from the ticket window to the main entrance, with the museum ahead of you. Use the front camera (try 0.5x if your phone has it) and keep the model over your shoulder. For a calmer selfie, the prayer-flag stupa just outside the museum is a quiet spot with flags hanging above it.
card.rules_and_safety: The museum has a ticketed entrance and the outdoor grounds may need a ticket too, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Get a statue, the building and the mountains all in one frame, then count your three layers out loud like a proud tour guide.
card.good_to_know: The International Mountain Museum opened on 5 February 2004. Inside are three main halls (Great Himalayas, Fame and World Mountains) plus an exhibition about the Yeti. Outside you'll find a "living museum" about Nepal's indigenous tribes and a 31-foot replica of Mt Manaslu.

selfie_research.notes: No page I found says which spot has the museum building directly behind the person, so the 'landmark behind' framing is my reading, not a verified viewpoint. No page names a spot where a passer-by should stand to photograph a visitor with the whole museum in frame, so I left ask_someone_spot null. A review says the outside yak statue can be climbed for photos, but that is a single user review and I did not include it as a spot. Heights for the Manaslu model conflict across sources (about 9.5 to 10 m, or 30 to 31 ft). No page I found gives selfie stick or tripod rules; one page says photography is generally permitted inside the museum, which is not a selfie-stick rule. No safety point was stated on the pages I found. Coordinates were not checked against a map.
